source.title: Attachment to God, Contingent Self-Worth, and Mental Health Outcomes in U.S. Collegiate Athletes

paper.citation: Upenieks, L., Bounds, E. M., Melton, K. K., Glanzer, P., & Schnitker, S. A. (2024). Attachment to God, contingent self-worth, and mental health outcomes in U.S. collegiate athletes. Journal of Religion and Health, 63(1), 445–465. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10943-023-01907-3
paper.abstract: How are secure, avoidant, and anxious attachment to God associated with depressive and anxiety symptoms among U.S. collegiate athletes, and does contingent self-worth based on others' approval statistically mediate those associations? The analytic sample was 415 U.S. intercollegiate varsity athletes drawn from a 1,930-student study at religious institutions or secular institutions with adjacent Christian study centers. Thirty-one percent competed in football or basketball; the paper grouped most other sports together and included athletes from Division I and Division III contexts. The sample and measures were predominantly situated in Christian religiosity. Preregistered cross-sectional analysis of wave-one online survey data from a larger longitudinal faith-and-character study. Depressive and anxiety symptoms were measured with the PHQ-9 and GAD-7; religious attachment used secure, avoidant, and anxious God Attachment Scale subscales; contingent self-worth used the Others' Approval subscale. Multivariable regression and Sobel-Goodman mediation models adjusted for demographic, academic, NCAA-division, and institutional covariates.
paper.tldr: This study addresses a less commonly examined dimension of collegiate-athlete well-being: how religious attachment and dependence on others' approval relate to self-reported depression and anxiety. Avoidant attachment to God was associated with higher depressive symptoms (b=0.16, p<.001), and anxious attachment was also associated with higher depressive symptoms (b=0.22, p<.01) in separate models; when all attachment styles entered together, only avoidant attachment remained significant (b=0.23, p<.05). Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Preregistered cross-sectional analysis of wave-one online survey data from a larger longitudinal faith-and-character study. Depressive and anxiety symptoms were measured with the PHQ-9 and GAD-7; religious attachment used secure, avoidant, and anxious God Attachment Scale subscales; contingent self-worth used the Others' Approval subscale. Multivariable regression and Sobel-Goodman mediation models adjusted for demographic, academic, NCAA-division, and institutional covariates.
paper.findings: Avoidant attachment to God was associated with higher depressive symptoms (b=0.16, p<.001), and anxious attachment was also associated with higher depressive symptoms (b=0.22, p<.01) in separate models; when all attachment styles entered together, only avoidant attachment remained significant (b=0.23, p<.05). The estimated indirect association of secure attachment with lower depressive symptoms through lower approval-contingent self-worth was b=-0.03 (p=.045), approximately 12% of the overall association. The corresponding indirect association for anxious attachment and higher depressive symptoms was b=0.04 (p=.043), approximately 14%; the avoidant-attachment indirect effect for depression was not significant (p=.343). For anxiety, indirect effects through contingent self-worth were significant for secure (b=-0.03, p=.045), avoidant (b=0.02, p=.012), and anxious attachment (b=0.04, p=.026), estimated as 11%, 12%, and 17% of their respective associations.
paper.limitations: Cross-sectional data cannot establish temporal or causal ordering; depression or anxiety may influence religious attachment and approval-contingent self-worth rather than the proposed direction. The 45–60-minute survey creates possible fatigue, although measure order was randomized and the authors reported good response quality. Predominantly Christian framing limits transfer to athletes from other faith traditions or without religious belief. Sport, captaincy, playing time, sport-specific pressures, injury status, and Division I versus Division III differences were not examined in sufficient detail. Statistical mediation in cross-sectional observational data is not evidence of a mechanism or treatment effect.
paper.practicalImplications: Religious or spiritual identity may be relevant when an athlete wants it included in care, but these findings do not support screening athletes by faith style or prescribing religious practice. Use athlete-led, culturally humble conversation and established mental-health referral pathways. Approval-contingent self-worth may be a useful discussion prompt, not a diagnosis or causal explanation.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. Religious or spiritual identity may be relevant when an athlete wants it included in care, but these findings do not support screening athletes by faith style or prescribing religious practice. Use athlete-led, culturally humble conversation and established mental-health referral pathways. Approval-contingent self-worth may be a useful discussion prompt, not a diagnosis or causal explanation. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: This study did not directly evaluate rehabilitation or return to sport. It provides no standalone clearance criterion, reinjury threshold, or validated return-to-play progression.
